verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, upon Mahalath, a Maskil, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the leader of the singers. Set to the tune called Mahalath. A song of insight, from David.
verses.directors_commentary: This line is the label on the scroll, not part of the song, and the Hebrew numbering counts it as verse 1. That is why the KJV is one number behind here: it prints the heading unnumbered as 'verse 0' and starts the song at 53:1. The KJV also tidied three unclear Hebrew terms. 'Chief Musician' is the choirmaster (the one who 'leads' or 'excels', from נצח). 'Mahalath' stays a transliterated name because no one knows what it meant. Rashi and Metzudat Zion take it as the name of an instrument; Meiri hears a root meaning 'sickness', a mournful key; YLT's 'On a disease' follows that route. 'Maskil' comes from the root 'to be wise, to act with insight', so it is a 'poem of insight' or a skilled song, and it quietly sets up the word 'insightful' in verse 3. Direct the reading as a hymn leader would cue a choir: this is liturgy to be sung, not a private lament.

philological_notes.note: A musical direction of unknown meaning. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read an instrument name; Meiri a melody of sadness from a root 'illness'. The same heading appears over Psalm 88.
Maskil, from 'to act wisely'. Metzudat David glosses it 'said with great understanding'. Whether it names a genre or a manner of performing is not settled.

verses.translation_literal: Said [the] fool in his heart: There-is-no God. They have acted-corruptly and have made-abominable wrong; there-is-none doing good.
verses.translation_dramatic: The fool has spoken, and not aloud. He has said it in the dark of his own heart, where no one can answer him: There is no God. And see what grows from that silence. Rot. They have fouled their ways, and made a stench of injustice; there is not one among them who does good.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play the fool as a man at ease, not a ranting atheist. Hebrew נָבָל is not a thinker who got his logic wrong. It is the coarse, shameless man, the Nabal of the Samuel story, who has no use for obligations. 'In his heart' means in his inner deliberation, the place where Hebrew thinking happens, and the sentence is a private calculation, not a speech. אֵין אֱלֹהִים is a practical denial: nobody above is watching or judging, so nothing is owed. Metzudat David reads it as 'everything is chance', and the Targum has 'there is no God who takes vengeance'. Every other line in the scene follows from that: if no one will call you to account, you may eat the weak.

The KJV's 'Corrupt are they' turns only the first verb, הִשְׁחִיתוּ, into an adjective, a state they happen to be in. The Hebrew says they did it: 'they have acted corruptly', a deed, and in the second verb they actively made things abominable. The KJV then renders the second verb as 'have done abominable iniquity', which treats עָוֶל ('wrong') as a direct object. That is how the Hebrew reads on its face. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as missing a ב: 'they made their way abominable in wrong' (Ibn Ezra on Ps 53:2; Radak on Ps 53:2). Meiri compares Ps 14:1, which has עֲלִילָה ('deed') here, and gives the sense as 'they made their way abominable through effort'. Ps 14 says YHWH where this psalm has Elohim, the mark of the Elohistic collection. The KJV's 'iniquity' also hides the root: עָוֶל is what crooked scales and crooked courts do, the opposite of a straight measure. Rashi, strikingly, makes the fool Titus, the man who sliced the curtain with a sword dripping blood and said he had killed God (Rashi on Ps 53:2, citing Gittin 56b). The audience would hear the sentence as an accusation of the powerful, not as a debating point.

philological_notes.note: Not 'intellectually stupid' but morally dull, one who has withered or fallen from obligations; the root is also 'to wilt'. Metzudat Zion calls him 'a low and contemptible man'. KJV 'fool' is acceptable but too mild.

The verb is a Hiphil and means to make abominable, not simply to commit. Ibn Ezra and Radak supply ב, 'in wrong', since the verb does not normally take a direct object. Without the ב, the KJV makes 'iniquity' the product of the act.

verses.translation_literal: Elohim from heaven looks down upon the sons of Adam, to see: is there one who acts with insight, one who seeks Elohim?
verses.translation_dramatic: But God leans out over the rim of heaven and looks down on the children of Adam. He is searching. Is there even one who sees clearly, one who goes looking for God?
verses.directors_commentary: After the fool's whisper, the camera pulls up and the point of view changes: God looks down. The verb הִשְׁקִיף is not a glance but a long bent look out of a window or over a parapet, the look of someone who leans from a high place; Metzudat Zion calls it a look with the intention of the heart. The KJV 'looked down' is fine but puts it in the past; the Hebrew is a present, ongoing scene. 'Sons of Adam' is the whole human race, which the KJV renders 'children of men'. Meiri notes that the phrase can carry a sense of the common crowd. The test of the inspection is the word מַשְׂכִּיל, 'one who acts with insight', the same root as the heading's 'Maskil'. The KJV's 'understand' makes it intellectual; here it means practical insight that shows itself in seeking God (דרש, the verb of consulting and inquiring at a sanctuary). Both ends of the verse pair the word Elohim, which the Psalter's editor uses for God throughout this psalm. Speak it slowly: the tension is the question, left hanging.

philological_notes.note: To bend and look out of a high place such as a window or the heavens. Metzudat Zion: 'a look with intention of the heart'.
Here a participle, 'one who acts with insight'. It repeats the root of the heading, and Malbim reads it as 'one who has good sense to grasp God'.
To seek, inquire, consult; the verb for approaching God at the sanctuary or through a prophet. Metzudat David: to search and inquire so as to know God's providence over all.

verses.translation_literal: All of it has turned back; together they have become corrupt. There is none who does good; there is not even one.
verses.translation_dramatic: The verdict comes down. Every one has turned away. All of them together have gone sour. No one does good. Not one. Not even one.
verses.directors_commentary: God's search ends in one flat sentence. 'All of it' is singular in Hebrew (כֻּלּוֹ, 'all of him'), as if the whole human race were one body that has slid backward; the KJV 'every one of them' splits it into individuals. סָג is to turn back or to withdraw, and Metzudat Zion compares it to 'justice is turned backward' in Isaiah 59:14. Rashi hears a different word, 'dross' (סִיגִים) as in Ezekiel 22:18: they are the waste left after smelting. 'Filthy' in the KJV is the sense of נֶאֱלָחוּ, a rare verb found in only a handful of places; Metzudat Zion compares it with Job 15, 'abominable and corrupt'. The last half of the verse is a hammer: the same 'there is none who does good' as in verse 2, now capped with 'not even one', which Paul will quote in Romans 3. Deliver it as an unemotional report, and let the silence do the work.

philological_notes.note: To turn back, fall back. Metzudat Zion links it to Isaiah 59:14; Rashi derives it from 'dross' (Ezekiel 22:18).
To become foul or tainted, morally spoiled; a rare verb. Meiri connects it with another word for impurity in Ezekiel, Metzudat Zion with Job 15.

verses.translation_literal: Do they not know, the workers of wickedness, those who devour my people, they have eaten bread? Elohim they have not called on.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do they not know, these workers of wickedness? They devour my people the way they eat their bread, without a thought. And on God they never once call.
verses.directors_commentary: Now a human voice breaks in: 'my people'. The speaker is in the psalm itself, taking the side of the poor. 'Devour my people' is the image of predators and of economic exploitation, the rich who consume the livelihood of the poor; Metzudat David reads that the oppressors do it with no one to object, as casually as they eat. The KJV's 'as they eat bread' puts the comparison in the middle of the clause. In the Hebrew the order is blunt, 'those who devour my people, they have eaten bread', and the line can be read as a comparison or as a plain statement that eating people is their daily meal. Verb choices matter too: 'call' (קָרָא) is the word for invoking God in worship and need; the KJV's 'called upon' is accurate but misses that in a world where bread came from the god of the rains, to eat without calling on God was to deny the giver. Rashi and Malbim add the tradition that the wicked should have known fear. Play the first line as incredulity, the second as contempt.

philological_notes.note: 'Workers of trouble / wickedness', a stock label for the wicked in the Psalms; און can mean harm, trouble or idolatry.
The grammar is ambiguous: 'as they eat bread' (comparison) or 'they have eaten bread' (a separate statement). Metzudat David reads the comparison, with no one to protest.

verses.translation_literal: There they feared a fear [where] there-was not fear, for God has scattered [the] bones of [the one] encamping [against you]; you have put-[them]-to-shame, for God has rejected-them.
verses.translation_dramatic: There, in that very place, they were seized by terror. A terror such as had never been. For God has scattered the bones of the ones who camped against you, and they lie in the open, unburied, with no one to gather them. You have shamed them, and you did it because God had already cast them off.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the reversal after the long accusation of the verses before. The ones who ate God's people like bread are now themselves eaten by fear, and the scene turns on two words: שָׁם, 'there', pointing at a place, and פָּחֲדוּ־פַחַד, 'they feared a fear', a cognate construction that the KJV flattens into 'great fear'. Play the repeated root as a shiver that repeats. KJV 'where no fear was' also adds a word the Hebrew does not have: לֹא־הָיָה פַחַד is simply 'there was not [any] fear', and the traditional readings split on its sense. Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Metzudat David take it as 'a fear such as never was before', citing Isa 23:13 for the same idiom ('this people was not'), meaning there was none like it (Ibn Ezra on Ps 53:6; Meiri on Ps 53:6; Metzudat David on Ps 53:6). Rashi reads it as a fear like the first one that struck Belshazzar, and places the scattering in the redemption yet to come, with the bones of Jerusalem's besiegers rotting as in Zech 14:12 (Rashi on Ps 53:6). The KJV's 'where no fear was' (and the ASV's, Webster's and BBE's versions of it) points the other way, panic where there was nothing to fear, and so it cannot be reconciled with the Belshazzar or 'never before' readings.

The historical settings are many. Metzudat David sets it in Jerusalem under Sennacherib, whose army fell as corpses, and on הֱבִישׁוֹתָה he adds Titus, whose slaughter and destruction shamed Israel because the Lord had then rejected them for their evil deeds, so that it was no accident. Meiri sees Nebuchadnezzar and his son, and the end of days with Gog and Magog (Ezek 38:22); Radak has Gog too; Rashi has the future redemption. Whichever you choose, the bones matter. To the ancient hearer, bones scattered and unburied were the worst fate for an army: no grave, no name, no rest. The verb פִּזַּר is a perfect where the sense is future for Meiri, a prophetic perfect, as the psalm sees the event as already done. 'You have put them to shame' uses a second-person verb, הֱבִשֹׁתָה, whose addressee is disputed: Ibn Ezra and Radak have David or the Messiah; Rashi has the Lord. KJV 'despised' for מְאָסָם is too emotional; the verb means to reject, to throw away as unfit, which is why ASV's 'rejected' is nearer.

philological_notes.note: A cognate accusative: 'they feared a fear'. The KJV's 'great fear' gives the intensity but drops the echo. The second פַחַד reappears in the clause 'there was not fear'.

A participle of 'to encamp' with the second-person suffix, 'the one encamping against you'. Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as a collective for the besiegers. Rashi records the reading of Dunash from חנך 'to train', which none of the others adopt.
To reject, to refuse as worthless. The sense is a judicial rejection, not an emotion; 'despised' (KJV) shifts it toward contempt.

verses.translation_literal: Who will give from Zion the salvations of Israel? When Elohim returns the captivity of his people, let Jacob be glad, let Israel rejoice.
verses.translation_dramatic: Who will send it out of Zion, the rescue of Israel? When God turns back the captivity of his people, let Jacob be glad, let Israel rejoice.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends in a prayer. 'Who will give' (מִי יִתֵּן) is the Hebrew way to say 'if only', 'would that': a wish. The KJV 'Oh that' gets it right. 'Salvations' is plural, a word for deliverance in every form, which the KJV flattens to 'salvation'. Zion is where help is imagined to come from because God's house is there. The idiom 'turn the captivity' (שׁוּב שְׁבוּת) is easily misread: it may mean 'bring the exiles home', which is how the KJV, Radak and Malbim take it, or 'turn the fortunes', restore what was lost, and it works even for a people never in exile; Metzudat David reads it as God quieting and settling his people. The last two clauses have two names for one people, with two verbs for joy, so the verbs are jussive wishes, 'let Jacob be glad', where the KJV's 'shall rejoice' is a plain future. Malbim, who takes Jacob as the exiled north and Israel as Judah, finds that the first verb marks a new event. Deliver it as a closing hymn line, hopeful and unsure.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'who will give', an idiom of wishing, 'would that'. Metzudat David: 'may the salvation of Israel come quickly'.
'Captivity' or 'fortunes': the phrase שׁוּב שְׁבוּת means to restore. Metzudat Zion derives it from the root of 'return'.
Two verbs of joy, two names of the people, in parallel. The forms are jussive or imperfect. Malbim distinguishes them as new joy versus lasting joy.
